title: Manchester's mill district Rising
premise: In 1847, Marguerite Eastwick, an apprentice clockmaker who has survived Manchester's mill district by learning which silences keep people safe, is summoned to repair the observatory's master clock just as the only bridge out of the district closes for the season. Trapped inside the mill owner's compound, they discover the clock's mechanism has been deliberately sabotaged to falsify working hours — a fraud that shortchanges hundreds of mill workers and conceals a fatal accident. As Marguerite repairs the work under the watchful eye of the owner's son, Edmund Harrow, whose conscience wars with his inheritance, they must choose between finishing the job and staying silent, or exposing the truth while the workshop still stands. The novel ends with Marguerite testifying before the factory commissioners as the bridge reopens, having lost their apprenticeship but gained a new trade of their own — and Edmund, stripped of his name, walking beside them into a city that will not easily forgive either of them.
about_author: Lior Yarrow is the pen name of a former industrial archivist who spent a decade cataloguing mill workers' ledgers in northern England before turning to fiction. Their writing is known for rendering machinery with tenderness and silence with menace.

chapters.title: The Weight of Small Gears
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. In the cramped workshop of Master Fenwick, Marguerite repairs a pocket watch for a mill overseer and notices the man flinch at the word 'hours.' Establishes the rules of survival: don't ask, don't repeat, don't look up. Emotional beat: watchful quiet, the loneliness of someone fluent in silence.

chapters.title: A Summons in Winter Light
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. A liveried messenger brings a commission from Harrow Mills: repair the observatory's master clock, the district's official timekeeper, before the quarter audits. Fenwick accepts on Marguerite's behalf without asking them. Emotional beat: dread dressed as opportunity; Marguerite senses the commission is larger than clocks.

chapters.title: Crossing Before the Ice
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. They cross the iron bridge with their tool chest as snow begins, watching workers haul the season's last cotton bales. A young weaver, Bess Carrick, warns them: 'Nothing good gets fixed inside those walls.' Emotional beat: the threshold moment — crossing from the free side of the river into the gilded cage.

chapters.title: The Observatory at Dusk
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. First sight of the master clock — a cathedral of brass — and first meeting with Edmund Harrow, who inspects their tools personally and asks oddly personal questions about Fenwick's other commissions. Emotional beat: wary fascination; two people measuring each other like unfamiliar mechanisms.

chapters.title: What the Escapement Remembers
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Opening the clock's case, Marguerite finds fresh file marks on the escapement — deliberate tampering, done by a skilled hand, making the clock run four minutes slow per day. Four minutes an hour, stolen from every worker's wage. Emotional beat: cold horror; the craft they love turned into a weapon.

chapters.title: Silence Is a Currency
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, with a flashback to three years earlier when Fenwick taught them which silences keep people safe after a colleague vanished for asking questions. Marguerite weighs repairing the clock honestly against what happened to the last apprentice who noticed too much. Emotional beat: fear calcifying into habit.

chapters.title: Edmund's Ledger
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Edmund reviews the mill accounts and finds the discrepancy he half-suspected: his father's manager, Cobbett, has been skimming wages through falsified time for years, with his father's tacit blessing. He burns nothing, tells no one, but copies figures by candlelight. Emotional beat: inherited guilt beginning to curdle into resolve.

chapters.title: Bess in the Stairwell
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Marguerite encounters Bess again in the observatory stairwell; Bess is there delivering mended linens and mentions her brother died in a loom accident last spring — an accident the mill recorded as happening 'outside working hours.' Emotional beat: grief finding language; the sabotage acquires a human face.

chapters.title: The Repair Begins
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Under Cobbett's supervision, Marguerite begins the official repair — restoring the clock to its sabotaged state while privately machining a true escapement part hidden in their coat lining. Edmund watches, saying little. Emotional beat: double life; every honest gesture now carries a dishonest weight.

chapters.title: Cobbett's Courtesy
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Cobbett invites Marguerite to dinner, praises their discretion, and doubles the fee — then mentions, pleasantly, how quickly Fenwick's last assistant found work in Liverpool. The threat is unmistakable and deniable. Emotional beat: terror wearing velvet gloves; the price of survival made explicit.

chapters.title: The Bridge Closes
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Ice on the river forces the bridge's seasonal closure; the district is sealed until thaw. Marguerite realizes there is no leaving, no sending word to Fenwick, no retreat. That night they finish the true escapement part anyway. Emotional beat: claustrophobia transmuted into commitment — trapped, they stop planning escape and start planning witness.

chapters.title: Two Kinds of Time
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Edmund confronts Marguerite in the observatory at midnight, having discovered the hidden true part. Instead of betraying them, he confesses what he knows of the ledgers and his brother's death cover-up. Emotional beat: the novel's central alliance forms — love and duty pulling in opposite directions, briefly aligned.

chapters.title: The Accident File
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Edmund retrieves the suppressed report on the loom accident from his father's study, nearly caught by Cobbett. He learns the machine was knowingly left unrepaired to save cost. Emotional beat: the moment inheritance becomes unbearable; power revealed as corruption passed down like a watch.

chapters.title: Fenwick's Letter
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. A smuggled letter from Fenwick arrives via a coal cart: 'Finish the work. Say nothing. Come home whole.' Marguerite understands it as both protection and instruction to stay complicit. They write no reply. Emotional beat: loyalty tested against conscience; the mentor's love revealed as another kind of cage.

chapters.title: Installing the Truth
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. During the quarterly audit inspection, Marguerite installs the true escapement — the clock will now keep honest time, and the audit will expose the wage fraud arithmetically. Cobbett signs off, unaware. Emotional beat: exhilaration laced with dread; the point of no return, disguised as routine craftsmanship.

chapters.title: Discovery
chapters.summary: Cobbett's POV. Cobbett discovers the swapped part during a routine winding, compares it against his private records, and understands everything. He locks down the observatory, accuses Marguerite of sabotage and theft, and sends for the magistrate. Emotional beat: the trap snapping shut; power moving swiftly and without apology.

chapters.title: The Workshop Still Stands
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Held in the mill's counting house, Marguerite learns Cobbett plans to burn Fenwick's workshop as 'evidence destruction' once Marguerite confesses. Bess organizes the weavers to stand witness outside. Emotional beat: desperation sharpening into solidarity; Marguerite's silence finally broken aloud.

chapters.title: Edmund's Choice
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Edmund presents his father with the copied ledgers and the accident file, offering him the chance to confess first. His father refuses and disowns him on the spot. Edmund walks out carrying the only copy of the evidence. Emotional beat: duty inverted — loyalty to truth over blood; love declared through action, not words.

chapters.title: The Magistrate's Room
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. Before the magistrate and the factory commissioner, Cobbett lays out his case. Marguerite, instead of confessing, demonstrates the sabotage with the clock's own mechanism before the assembled room — showing the filed marks, the arithmetic of stolen minutes, the dead weaver's misrecorded hours. Emotional beat: the climax; craft as testimony, silence transformed into speech.

chapters.title: What the Clock Struck
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. The commissioner orders an inquiry; Cobbett is arrested attempting to flee across the frozen river; the elder Harrow collapses, his empire of small thefts laid bare. Bess's testimony about her brother lands hardest. Emotional beat: catharsis without triumph — justice arriving late, partial, and real.

chapters.title: Thaw
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV. The bridge reopens. Fenwick takes Marguerite back but Marguerite chooses instead to take a journeyman's post with the commissioners' office, certifying public clocks — keeping honest time as a trade. Edmund, nameless now, asks to be taught the lathe. Emotional beat: quiet resolution; the price paid tallied, and worth it.

chapters.title: Keeping Honest Hours
chapters.summary: Marguerite's POV, one year later. Marguerite winds the observatory clock each Sunday, now publicly accountable, while Bess trains new weavers and Edmund finishes his first commissioned piece — a small watch engraved with a bridge. The district still remembers, still resents, still endures. Emotional beat: earned peace; love against duty resolved into love as duty, kept like time itself.
